chapter: Berlin and the Turner and Bryant bands
title: Willy Bryant's band, a telegram from Paris, and the Oglethorpe incident
summary: He was happy touring the South with Willy Bryant until a telegram came to join Willy Lewis; in Oglethorpe, Georgia, Bryant drew a switchblade after a girl's remark and the band covered with Sweet Georgia Brown.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Excuse me, the Hank Jones that was playing piano --

Not the same one. This is the Hank Jones -- was a little fellow, little, small fellow. He come from Louisville, Kentucky. Small fellow. Someone said "Hank Jones is here." I made that mistake when I come back, but I knew there was another Hank Jones.

So I went with that band and I stayed there. And I got a telegram from Paris to come to join Willy Lewis's band. And I was happy with Willy Bryant's band. Very happy. We used to go traveling, all down South and there. And Willy Bryant was up there, looking like he looked, you know. And we went down to a place, Oglethorpe, Georgia. And a little

girl come up there and said, Mr. Bryant, you sure look good in front of all them niggers up there." Willy Bryant--he's in full dress --pull out a great long switchblade, and the trombone says, "Oh, Willy, master race." Oh, we're master race.

And then somebody starts off and plays "Sweet Georgia Brown" and I don't think the girl realized what she really had done. And I don't think none of those sheriffs or whatever they were, the people on the sidelines where the ropes were at, had seen what happened. We'd a been wasted. Oh, no, no, no, you start calling him talking about white folks, something like that, you got an enemy. Oh, no, you don't do that.
